turns.content:
- I had a squat session yesterday at 135 pounds, which is a weight I handled easily before my ankle sprain. I hesitated on the third rep and racked the bar early.

- Marcus told me my ankle is fully healed and I'm just babying it, letting mental hesitation stall an easy progression. He sounded dismissive.

- I've spent months doing eversion drills and eccentric heel drops alone in my living room. The joint still feels tight and vulnerable under load.

- Part of me thinks he might be right and I am making excuses. But another part feels angry that my caution was dismissed as cowardice.

I'm trying to figure out if my reaction is reasonable or if I'm being overly sensitive.

The reports you provided do not establish that your mixed reaction is “reasonable” or “overly sensitive.” Those are evaluative labels, not findings from the events given.

What is in the account: you squatted 135 lb (a load you say you handled easily before the sprain), hesitated on the third rep, and racked early. You report months of eversion drills and eccentric heel drops, and that the joint still feels tight and vulnerable under load. Marcus stated the ankle is fully healed and that you are babying it, with mental hesitation stalling an easy progression; you described the comments as sounding dismissive and reported both considering he might be right and anger at caution being treated as cowardice.

Healing status is unknown here. No exam findings, imaging, clearance date, or stated basis for Marcus’s “fully healed” claim are included. Your reported tightness and vulnerability under load is one data point; his statement is another. They are not resolved by calling the early rack mental stalling.

Treating the rack as proven excuses raises re-injury risk while the joint is still reported as tight and vulnerable under a previously easy load. Treating Marcus’s framing as the last word does not settle load tolerance.

A clinician or physical therapist assessment of the ankle under load would distinguish incomplete recovery from purely mental hesitation more reliably than this exchange. With Marcus, you can state the reported sensation and the early rack without accepting or arguing the “babying” characterization. Train to the reported joint response until that assessment exists; do not use the disagreement to decide the next 135 lb attempt.

- I appreciate that you didn't just tell me what I wanted to hear. That actually helps.

- You're right that there's no clinical assessment in what I described. Marcus isn't a PT, and he hasn't seen my ankle under load during a session.

- The tightness is real. It's not pain, it's a specific stiffness at the bottom of the squat that wasn't there before the sprain.

- I think what stung most was him reducing the months of work to me being mentally weak. Those drills were tedious and I did them alone.

Is asking for a modified progression until the stiffness resolves reasonable, or is that still making excuses?

The reports still do not classify asking for a modified progression as “reasonable” or as “making excuses.” Those remain labels, not findings.

You report new stiffness at the bottom of the squat (not pain), a previously easy 135 lb load, hesitation and an early rack on the third rep, months of isolated eversion and eccentric heel-drop work, and no clinician or PT exam of the ankle under squat load. Marcus did not observe that session and is not a PT. Effort on the drills does not establish current load tolerance; neither does his “fully healed / mental hesitation” account.

Requesting a change in depth, load, or volume while that stiffness is present matches training to a reported end-range limit. Calling the request excuses assumes the stiffness does not constrain the lift. That assumption is unverified.

Unknowns that matter: tissue status, available dorsiflexion and eversion under load, whether the stiffness predicts re-injury, and how long it would take to change. Unmodified 135 lb at full depth can repeat the early rack or increase sprain risk if a mechanical limit is still there. An open-ended “until it resolves” plan leaves duration and success criteria undefined and can delay useful loading or miss a treatable restriction.

Get the ankle assessed in squat-like positions. Until then, set depth or load so the reported stiffness is not what stops the set, and do not use the disagreement with Marcus as the rule for the next attempt.

- You mentioned getting the ankle assessed in squat-like positions. That makes sense, but the timeline matters here. My physio discharged me at week eight with full range of motion in dorsiflexion and no pain on single-leg tests.

- The stiffness only shows up under a loaded barbell at depth. I can bodyweight squat fine. I can do lunges fine.

- If the assessment says everything looks normal structurally, then what? Is this just a loading adaptation issue that needs gradual progression anyway?

I think that's what I'm trying to separate out. Am I dealing with a real mechanical limitation or a normal discomfort that I should push through?

Discharge at week eight with full dorsiflexion range of motion and pain-free single-leg tests does not classify the loaded-squat stiffness as a mechanical limit or as discomfort to push through.

Those tests, plus pain-free bodyweight squats and lunges, do not measure the ankle at the bottom of a barbell squat. You report stiffness only in that position, on a load (135 lb) that was previously easy, with an early rack on the third rep. That is a load-specific symptom after a sprain. It is not explained by the discharge tests, and it is not explained by Marcus’s account.

A later exam that looks “normal structurally” would still not settle the fork you named. Normal unloaded range and a clear structural screen would not show that the stiffness is harmless adaptation, and they would not show that repeating full-depth 135 lb is appropriate. Pushing through assumes the sensation is not a remaining constraint. That assumption is unverified. Treating the stiffness as a proven block that forbids all loading is also unverified.

Unknowns that would change the next session: time since discharge, loaded dorsiflexion at squat depth, and a clinician watching the ankle under the bar. None of those are in this history.

Until that assessment exists, set depth or load so the reported stiffness is not what ends the set. If an assessment later finds no structural problem, the remaining task is still how to load that end range, not to treat the early rack as mental hesitation or as a reason to ignore the symptom.

- I think I'm going to ask Marcus to back off the squat progression for two weeks while I get a loaded assessment done.

- But part of me wants to just quit his sessions entirely and find someone else who won't make me feel like I'm being weak for being careful.

- Is that an overreaction, or is his comment enough to justify switching trainers?

The reports do not establish that quitting is an overreaction or that Marcus’s comment is enough to require a switch.

What is on the record is one statement: that the ankle is fully healed and that you are babying it with mental hesitation. He is not a PT and did not see the loaded squat. That is not a pattern, a refused pause, or a finding about future sessions. Wanting to avoid that framing is a preference. It is not evidence that staying is unsafe or that leaving is required.

The squat constraint is separate. Stiffness only at the bottom under a barbell, an early rack at 135 lb, and discharge tests that did not include that position still support pausing full-depth loaded squats until a loaded assessment, not a two-week calendar. Two weeks is not a healing result. If the exam is later than that, the pause should follow the exam.

Tradeoffs: asking Marcus to hold squat progression pending that assessment tests whether he will train inside the reported limit and keeps continuity; he may repeat the same framing. Switching now ends that framing from him, costs a search, and does not by itself get the ankle assessed under the bar or guarantee a better loading plan. Continuing unmodified 135 lb at depth remains unverified against the stiffness.

Book the loaded assessment. State the limit in observable terms (stiffness at depth under the bar; early rack at 135 lb; no full-depth loaded squats until that exam). Do not argue weakness versus caution. Keep or leave Marcus as a working-relationship choice after you see whether that constraint is accepted; do not treat the single comment as the verdict.

- I think I need to figure out what to actually say to Marcus before next session.

- A loaded assessment is the real priority. I'll book that first and then talk to him.

- If I ask him to hold squat progression pending the exam, and he pushes back again, that tells me something different than one dismissive comment.

Would it be reasonable to say something like "I'm getting the ankle checked under load before I push past that stiffness point, so let's pause squats at 135 until I have results"?

The reports still do not classify the line as “reasonable.” That label is not a finding.

The content is usable if it states a decision and ties it to the exam, not if it asks Marcus to agree about stiffness, healing, or mental hesitation.

Your draft mixes a clear plan with a claim he can reopen: “before I push past that stiffness point.” That invites the same argument (push through vs baby it). The early rack at 135 lb and stiffness only at loaded depth are already on the record. The pause does not need his theory of why.

Say the constraint in observable terms. Do not litigate weakness.

Sendable:

“I’m booking an assessment of the ankle under load. Until I have those results, I won’t do full-depth squats at 135. We can use less depth, a lighter load, or other lower-body work.”

That matches what is known: discharge tests did not include a loaded barbell at depth; stiffness showed up there; the next step is that exam. It does not claim a structural injury, a two-week healing window, or that 135 lb is forbidden in every variation.

Book the assessment first, as you said. Deliver that limit as a working rule for the session, not as a debate. One pushback would be a second data point about whether he will train inside it; it would not, by itself, settle whether to switch trainers.
